questions.question: The general sibling combinator '~' selects:

options.text: All following siblings (not just adjacent) matching the selector

questions.explanation: ~ targets later siblings; + is adjacent-only. Both require the element to follow the reference in the same parent.

questions.question: input:not([disabled]) selects:

options.text: All input elements WITHOUT the disabled attribute

questions.explanation: :not() negates a selector; here it excludes disabled inputs — handy for styling active form fields.

questions.question: A combinator list 'ul li' (space) means:

options.text: Any li that is a DESCENDANT of a ul (any depth)
ul that is a child of li

questions.explanation: The descendant combinator (space) matches any nested level. Use '>' for direct children only.

questions.question: Which selector has the LOWEST specificity?
questions.explanation: Universal * has zero specificity. IDs are highest among these; classes beat elements.

questions.question: a[href^='https'] targets links whose href:
questions.explanation: ^= starts-with, $= ends-with, *= contains. Useful to style external vs internal links.

questions.question: :is() (formerly :any) is useful because it:

options.text: Groups selectors and takes the SPECIFICITY OF ITS MOST SPECIFIC ARGUMENT

questions.explanation: :is(h1,h2,h3) simplifies grouping; its specificity equals the strongest inner selector (unlike :where which is 0).

questions.question: :where() differs from :is() in that it:

options.text: Always has ZERO specificity (great for reset-like rules)

questions.explanation: :where() zero-specificity makes grouped selectors easy to override later — ideal for base/resets without raising specificity.

questions.question: ::before and ::after create:

options.text: Generated content boxes as the first/last child of the selected element

questions.explanation: Pseudo-elements inject decorative content via content:''; require content (even empty) to render. Double-colon is modern syntax.
